Publisher Summary text
This chapter discusses the group frequencies of alcohols and phenols in infrared (IR) and Raman spectra. The characteristic vibrations involving the O —H grouping are the stretching and bending modes of the O—H and C—Ο moieties. The vibrational spectra of phenol and substituted phenols are subject to extensive studies. The O—H stretching band in the IR spectrum is by far the most characteristic IR band of alcohols and phenols. The free O—H vibration occurs as a sharp IR band at above 3600 cm-<sup>1</sup> while for the majority of condensed-phase samples, this O—H band is broadened and shifted to 3500–2500
equation_inline
\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }
text
because of the various types of hydrogen bond formation. Characteristically, the presence of this sharp or broad band suggests a good possibility of the presence of the OH group. The chapter discusses the free O —H stretching in phenols. The O—H stretching frequencies of para- and meta-substituted phenols in vapor phase appear as a single band in the region of 3660–3642 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

4-2.3 Hydrogen Bonded O—H Stretching text
Hydrogen bonding arises from the interaction between the OH proton and the lone-pair or π electrons of a nearby basic site. Examples for the basic sites include nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, and halogen atoms and functional groups that contain π electrons. The interaction can be either intermolecular or intramolecular. Infrared spectroscopy has been an excellent technique to study hydrogen bonding. The ef ect of hydrogen bond formation is to increase the IR intensity and lower the O—H stretching frequency. Generally, the stronger the hydrogen bond, the more the OH stretching frequency is shifted to a lower frequency. text
The strength of intermolecular hydrogen bonding depends on the local molecular structure [54, 70], concentration, solvent, and temperature[69, 71, 72]. The hydrogen bond strength increases as the basicity of the lone electron-pair hydrogen-bond acceptor site increases, and as the acidity of the hydrogen-bond donor hydrogen increases. The spectral position and intensity of the O—H stretching mode are infl uenced by these factors. The extent of intermolecular hydrogen bond interaction decreases with solute concentrations, and the hydrogen bond strength is minimized in the vapor phase or in dilute

A benzene ring —monosubstituted with a halogen—has a total of 30 modes of vibration. equation_inline

text
or so of a given average wave number and can be considered to be group frequencies. Each mode has its own rules about IR or Raman intensity or wave number shift with mass or inductive or mesomeric ef ects of the substituents. This makes the substituted benzenes some of the most complex groups encountered. The chapter illustrates the major substituent-insensitive mono-, di-, and tri-substituted benzene IR and Raman bands. The out-of-plane C—H wag vibrations give rise to the most useful IR bands and are used to distinguish dif erent types of aromatic ring substitution.

As seen in Fig. 17-2, the quadrant stretch modes interact somewhat with in-plane CH bend, and this interaction is strong in the two semicircle stretch modes. Tangentially moving carbons and their hydrogens move in roughly opposite directions. Radially moving carbons and their hydrogens move in nearly the same direction. Substituents are nearly motionless. text
Unsubstituted benzene at equilibrium has a center of symmetry. As seen in Fig. 17-2, one can start at any atom and go in a straight line through the center and an equal distance beyond, where one will fi nd a symmetrically equivalent atom. In the vibrationally distorted molecule, the atoms move to the tips of the displacement vectors. As seen in Fig. 17-2a, the vibrationally distorted benzene performing either quadrant stretch vibration retains the center of symmetry. (Vector tip pairs are seen on the opposite sides of the center.) This means these vibrations in benzene, or in centrosymmetrically substituted benzenes, are IR-inactive. Therefore, symmetrically substituted para- (1,4), tetra- (1, 2, 4, 5), or hexasubstituted benzenes show no quadrant-stretch IR absorption bands near 1600 and 1580 cm<sup>−1</sup>. These are all Raman-active, however [5, 19].

Publisher Summary

text
This chapter discusses the group frequencies of alcohols and phenols in infrared (IR) and Raman spectra. The characteristic vibrations involving the O —H grouping are the stretching and bending modes of the O—H and C—Ο moieties. The vibrational spectra of phenol and substituted phenols are subject to extensive studies. The O—H stretching band in the IR spectrum is by far the most characteristic IR band of alcohols and phenols. The free O—H vibration occurs as a sharp IR band at above 3600 cm-<sup>1</sup> while for the majority of condensed-phase samples, this O—H band is broadened and shifted to 3500–2500
equation_inline
\mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }
text
because of the various types of hydrogen bond formation. Characteristically, the presence of this sharp or broad band suggests a good possibility of the presence of the OH group. The chapter discusses the free O —H stretching in phenols. The O—H stretching frequencies of para- and meta-substituted phenols in vapor phase appear as a single band in the region of 3660–3642 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

4-2.3 Hydrogen Bonded O—H Stretching

text
Hydrogen bonding arises from the interaction between the OH proton and the lone-pair or π electrons of a nearby basic site. Examples for the basic sites include nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, and halogen atoms and functional groups that contain π electrons. The interaction can be either intermolecular or intramolecular. Infrared spectroscopy has been an excellent technique to study hydrogen bonding. The ef ect of hydrogen bond formation is to increase the IR intensity and lower the O—H stretching frequency. Generally, the stronger the hydrogen bond, the more the OH stretching frequency is shifted to a lower frequency.

The CC bonds in benzene are all equivalent and are roughly a “bond-and-a-half.” Because of this equivalence, the coupled CC bonds all interact, and the ring is best considered as a whole. Colthup et al. [23] used a mechanical standing-wave type description for ring vibrations where nodal lines separate the parts of the ring that vibrate out-of-phase with each other. As seen in Fig. 17-2a, there are two vibrations that involve “quadrant” stretch. Two nodal lines separate the ring into quadrants, and the ring CC bonds that are predominantly in one quadrant stretch, while those in the neighboring quadrants contract. As seen in Fig. 17-2b there are two vibrations that involve “semicircle” stretch. One nodal line separates the ring into semicircles, and ring CC bonds that are predominantly in one semicircle stretch, while those in the other contract. A ring bond that is bisected by a nodal line does not change in length.

text
In mono- and disubstituted benzenes, the two quadrant stretch components usually give rise to bands at 1620-1585 and 1590-1565 cm<sup>−1</sup>. The second band is often weaker in the IR than the fi rst, but is sometimes enhanced by ring conjugation or halogen substitution. In the Raman spectra, the 1620-1565 cm<sup>−1</sup> bands are medium in intensity [5, 19]. In the IR, the intensities are variable [4]. When the ring is para-substituted with identical substituents, a center of symmetry is present that is retained during the quadrant stretch vibrations, making these vibrations IR-inactive. However, if the substituents para to each other are dif erent, these modes are IRallowed. The greater the dif erence between the electron-donating or -withdrawing character of the para substituents, the stronger the IR bands will be [4]. Meta-substituted rings have IR band intensities in this region that vary with the sum (rather than the dif erence) of the electronic ef ects of the substituents, and ortho-substituted aromatics are intermediate [4]. Monosubstituted benzenes have weak IR intensities for weakly interacting substituents such as
equation_inline
\mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { C l }
text
, but stronger IR intensities for electron donors or withdrawers [4]. The wavenumbers for substituents such as Cl or S are at the lower end of the given regions, not because of the heavier mass (these atoms are nearly stationary) but because the
equation_inline
\scriptstyle \mathbf { C } - \mathbf { C l } { \mathrm { ~ o r ~ } } \mathbf { C } - \mathbf { S }
text
stretching and bending force constants (involved to some extent) are somewhat lower.
